SCGSim turns your layout into a 3D model that a solver can mesh. You give it
three things: the layout's polygons, usually from a GDSFactory component; the
PDK's layer stack, which says what material each layer is and at which height;
and the Nets, which say which pieces of metal are one conductor. From these,
SGB, SCGSim's semantic geometry builder, builds the model: the substrate, the
metal and the vacuum around them, with named faces for ports, junctions and
Surface EPR. Palace meshes this model with Gmsh; HFSS and Q3D import the same
model as a STEP file.

This page follows one small example through the steps, small enough that every
number can be checked by hand: two pieces of metal a few micrometres across,
one with a hole and a notch, on Net A and Net B, over a silicon substrate with
vacuum around them, and a junction requested between them. A real chip is
hundreds of micrometres across; the steps are the same. The page stops at the
built model; the mesh is on [Mesh and numerics](model-and-numerics.qmd).

## 1. What goes into the model {#source-stage}

A layout outline answers "where is the drawn shape?". It does not answer
"what material is here?", "which conductor does it belong to?" or "what is on
top of it?". SCGSim keeps those answers as declared facts, so that no later
step has to guess them from names or from which shapes are close.

### Three sources {#three-sources-contribute-different-facts}

| Source | Supplies | In this example |
|---|---|---|
| Component (often a GDSFactory component) | Polygons and holes, the names of its parts, and marked sheets such as a junction's port sheet | A notched left metal with a hole, and a sheet for the junction |
| PDK | For each layer: material, role, Z range and thickness | A metal film on a Si substrate, surrounded by vacuum |
| Assembly | Where each component is placed, the final Nets, the substrate and vacuum regions, how films become solver geometry, and requests such as a junction | `chip/left` on Net A, `chip/right` on Net B, the `substrate_face` profile and a rectangular junction |

A component's declarations stay local to it; it does not decide the Net of
each placed copy. Facts that span components, such as Nets and regions, belong
to the assembly.

### One example {#follow-one-model-before-looking-at-its-records}

The left metal has six outer corners, one enclosed hole and a notch open to the
outside. The right metal is a separate piece. The assembly puts them on Net A
and Net B over a Si substrate and surrounds them with vacuum.
@fig-sgb-source shows the left polygon; @fig-sgb-source-context places both
metals in the same frame.

::: {#fig-sgb-source .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-source-xy.html" title="Source polygon: six exterior corners and four hole corners" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

The left source polygon. P1–P6 mark its exterior and H1–H4 its hole;
coordinates are in µm.
:::

```text
Outer ring: P1(-2,0) → P2(3,0) → P3(3,1) → P4(2,1)
            → P5(2,2) → P6(-2,2) → back to P1
Hole ring:  H1(-1.5,0.5) → H2(-0.5,0.5) → H3(-0.5,1.5)
            → H4(-1.5,1.5) → back to H1
Units: µm
```

The bounding rectangle is 10 µm². Removing the 1 µm² notch and the 1 µm² hole
leaves 8 µm² of metal. Moving the component changes where it sits in the
assembly, and changing its Net changes an electrical declaration; neither edits
the polygon.

::: {#fig-sgb-source-context .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-context-xy.html" title="Both metal sources and their assembly position" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

Both metals in the assembly frame, with the substrate and the vacuum around
them.
:::

### Entity, occurrence, Net and snapshot {#entity-occurrence-and-net}

The named object `chip/left` is an **Entity**: a stable name for a declared
shape with its role and material. The substrate and the vacuum are Entities
too, so an Entity is not necessarily a conductor. A **Net** is a named piece of
metal that acts as one conductor: the assembly maps `chip/left` to Net A and
`chip/right` to Net B. A Net is your declaration; it does not say that shapes
touch.

A component placed in the layout is an **occurrence**. Two copies of one
component share their design but have different occurrence paths and
placements, so the prepared model can tell which placed pad a port or contact
belongs to.

`plan.prepare()` collects all of this into a **snapshot**: a fixed copy of the
polygons, Entities, occurrences, layer stack, Nets, physical representation
and port or junction requests. Later edits to the component do not change a
snapshot; prepare again to take them in.

| Term | What it names | Why it is kept separate |
|---|---|---|
| Polygon and ring | An outline, its holes and the order of its corners | A shape does not say what material or conductor it is |
| Entity | A named declared object and its role | Derived geometry can always be traced back to it |
| Occurrence | One placed copy, with its path and placement | Two copies of one component stay distinct |
| Net | Your grouping of metal into conductors | Shapes touching does not change it |
| Snapshot | One prepared copy of all of the above | Every later step reads the same fixed input |

Shapes of different Nets never merge, even where they touch: SCGSim stops with
an error instead. The exact contact rules are in the
[GeometryPlan reference](../reference/specs/geometry-plan.qmd#component-to-backend-geometry-contract).

Every XY coordinate of the assembled layout lies on one grid, the database unit
of the GDS the component was written to: 1 nm in this example (the
[case index](../images/sgb-concept/public-case-binding.json) records it).
SCGSim reads the unit from the GDS and changes no PDK or GDSFactory setting.
Heights, film thicknesses and mesh sizes are separate from this grid.

## 2. From layer stack to solver geometry {#planning-stage}

The layer stack says what the process contains. This step decides what this
solve will build from it: it applies the chosen film representation, finds the
interfaces between materials, and adds geometry only where you requested it.

### A film becomes a sheet or a block {#a-source-film-and-a-solver-sheet-are-different-things}

In this example the metal film occupies $z\in[0,0.25]$ µm. The assembly
chose Route A with the `substrate_face` profile, so the solver sees the metal
as a sheet of zero thickness on the substrate's top face at $z=0$. The film's
interval stays recorded as a process fact; the sheet is the solver's geometry.
Route B would keep the film as a 0.25 µm block instead;
[Route A and Route B](routes.qmd) compares the choices.

::: {#fig-sgb-physical .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-cross-section.html" title="Source film, Si substrate and vacuum; switch to the effective sheet view" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

A cross-section of the declared film and of the sheet the solver sees. Use the
controls to switch between them and to show the whole substrate and vacuum.
:::

In @fig-sgb-physical, Si occupies $z\in[-2,0]$ µm and the vacuum above it
$z\in[0,4.25]$ µm. `lower_air` is vacuum beside the substrate's side faces over
$z\in[-2,0]$ µm; there is no vacuum under the substrate in this example. These
regions tell SCGSim which material lies on each side of the sheet.

### A junction adds geometry only when requested {#a-junction-changes-geometry-only-when-requested}

A lumped port is a surface on which the solver applies a circuit element, here
the junction. A rectangular junction request names the port sheet and ties its
two ends to the Entities, occurrences and Nets of the metal on either side. It
is your request; SCGSim does not infer a junction from a visible gap.

The request asks for a complete rectangle between the two metals. The left
metal has a notch where the rectangle must meet it, so SCGSim adds a 1 µm²
piece over $[2,3]\times[1,2]$ µm to the left metal, on Net A. It does not
connect Net A and Net B. The right end belongs to Net B; the rectangle in the
middle is the port.

::: {#fig-sgb-effective .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-effective-xy.html" title="The requested left terminal support fills the notch and keeps its hole" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

The left metal after the request: the original outline for comparison, and in
orange the piece added for the junction.
:::

The left metal grows from 8 to 9 µm² and keeps its hole. The seam between the
original metal and the added piece lies inside the metal, so it is not an edge
of the model.

::: {#fig-sgb-effective-port .askr-wide-figure}
```{=html}
<iframe src="../images/sgb-concept/en-port-xy.html" title="Central rectangular port between two separately owned terminal supports" width="100%" height="640" style="border:0;" loading="lazy"></iframe>
```

The rectangular port and the metal of each end.
:::

The port spans $x\in[3,7]$ and $y\in[0,2]$ µm. Before building it, SCGSim
checks the named sheet, its overlap with each metal, the occurrences, the
Entities and the Nets. Without the request none of this geometry exists.

### One surface, two interfaces {#one-support-plane-can-describe-two-material-interfaces}

An interface is where two materials meet. The sheet of the left metal has Si
below it and vacuum above it, so it carries two interfaces: metal–substrate
(MS) and metal–air (MA). The bare substrate next to it is a third,
substrate–air (SA). MA and MS share the sheet's shape but not its sides or
materials, so their field energies are evaluated separately; see
[Surface EPR](surface-epr.qmd#interfaces).

## 3. Building and meshing {#construction-stage}

<span id="use-a-shared-planar-arrangement-to-determine-region-membership"></span>
<span id="sgb-writes-the-plan-it-already-owns"></span>
<span id="meshing-uses-the-built-geometry-and-its-own-sizing-recipe"></span>
<span id="fig-sgb-method-source-edges"></span>
<span id="fig-sgb-method-network"></span>
<span id="fig-sgb-method-arrangement"></span>
<span id="fig-sgb-method-shared-edge"></span>

SGB then builds the 3D model in three steps.

1. **Shared edges.** It splits every outline where it meets another, on the
   model grid, so that touching shapes share exactly the same edges and
   neighbouring faces share whole edges. No CAD Boolean decides which material
   owns a face.
2. **Files and sidecar.** It writes the model as BREP and XAO files for Gmsh,
   a STEP file for AEDT, and a **sidecar**: a JSON file that records which
   Entity, Net, interface and Surface-EPR band each face and volume of those
   files came from. Palace's attributes and AEDT's assignments are made from
   the sidecar.
3. **Mesh.** For Palace, Gmsh fills the model with tetrahedra. Where an element
   is too badly shaped, SCGSim refines the mesh around it and meshes again; if
   that does not succeed within its budget, `mesh()` stops with
   `MeshRepairError`. This holds for the default recipe and every recipe but
   `GmshDefaultRecipe()`, which meshes once without repair and delivers the
   mesh whatever its quality. A finer mesh changes the elements, not the model.

How SGB does each step, with worked examples, is on
[Geometry builder internals](../contribute/internals/geometry.qmd). The mesh
controls are in the
[Palace mesh reference](../reference/specs/palace-electrostatic-sgb.qmd#palace-mesh-controls).

## 4. Curves and bands {#distance-bands}

A polygon outline stays a polygon, even where it approximates an arc. Curves
you declare explicitly can be line segments and circular arcs, which SGB builds
exactly; any other kind of curve is refused with `UnsupportedCurveError`
([source curves](../reference/specs/geometry-plan.qmd#source-curves)).

Surface-EPR inset margins are cut into the model as bands when it is built;
[Surface EPR](surface-epr.qmd#surface-distance-band-correction) explains them
with this example's left metal. Every rule of the model is in the
[GeometryPlan reference](../reference/specs/geometry-plan.qmd).

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Where the example comes from"}
The example is the public test fixture `physical_fixture()` in
[`tests/test_rectangular_junction_geometry.py`](https://github.com/NCUPHY-LTLab/scgsim/blob/v3.0.0rc4/tests/test_rectangular_junction_geometry.py#L252),
with a 1 µm square hole added to the left metal for these figures. The
[case index](../images/sgb-concept/public-case-binding.json) records its
units, profile and which figure shows which step.
:::
